questions.q: What does a sliding-window backtest keep as training data at each origin?
options: All data up to the origin
The last W points before the origin
A random sample of past points
why: Correct: the window moves and keeps a fixed length.
Random samples break the order and are not a window.

options: The first date of the series
The last date you know when you make the forecast
The date with the largest error
why: Correct: everything after the origin is hidden.
The origin has nothing to do with error size.

questions.q: n = 100, initial = 60, horizon = 10, step = 10, no gap. How many complete folds?
questions.why: Origins at 60, 70, 80, 90. The test window of origin 90 is points 90 to 99, so it fits. 4 folds.

questions.q: n = 100, initial = 60, horizon = 10, step = 10, gap = 5. How many complete folds?
questions.why: Origins at 60, 70, 80 fit (test ends at 74, 84, 94). Origin 90 would need points up to 104. So 3 folds.

questions.q: Select all reasons to prefer many origins over one split.
options: The average is less affected by one lucky period
You can see if the error changes over time
You get a spread (min, max) of the error
why: Yes. One window can be easy or hard by chance.
Yes. You see drift and changes.
No. More folds mean more training runs, so it is slower.
Yes. The spread tells how stable the model is.

questions.q: Your pipeline gets sales data 3 days late. You retrain every Monday and forecast 14 days. Which backtest setting copies this?
why: It lets the backtest use the 3 newest days that production never has.
Correct: the last 3 days are missing at forecast time, so hide them.
The horizon stays 14. The delay is a gap, not a shorter horizon.

questions.q: A model has MAE 4.0 averaged over all steps of a 14-day horizon. A manager only needs day 1 to 3. What do you do?
options: Report the MAE of steps 1 to 3 from the backtest
why: The average mixes in far steps, which are harder.
Correct: horizon-wise errors show the quality for the steps that matter.
That changes the model, and may not be needed. First look at the step-wise error.
